risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the claim as worded. The first-year figures are primary data from random samples of one month's returnees, 95% interviewed, with self-reports checked against military records and urine taken at interview, by interviewers who did not know which men had used drugs (card sc_robins_1975: JBI moderate); concealment would lower the figures for use after return, and the authors judge it unlikely. The three-year figures, the treatment figures and Figure 6 come from the principal investigator's lecture (card sc_robins_1993: narrative-review checklist, high), which gives no total sample size, no definition of re-addiction and no intervals, and whose text and graphs disagree in places ('6% overall' against about 12% in Figure 6; 'nearly half' against about 61% using narcotics again); the statement gives the figures with their stated time frames and names the disagreements. Read strictly, the lecture-only figures would be rated down one level, to very low.

inconsistency.note: The 1975 report and the 1993 lecture describe one study and agree in direction; their differences (43% against 45% trying narcotics; about 2% and 7% in the two samples against 5% combined in the first year; 95% against 96% interviewed) lie within one study's reporting and are stated.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: young US Army enlisted men in Vietnam in 1970–71 and after return; the statement gives the principal investigator's own caution that the conditions were unprecedented and that few of the men would have become addicted at home, so nothing is generalized to people who become addicted in ordinary civilian life.

imprecision.note: No intervals are printed and some counts are small (about 2 of 90 men in the random sample's figure; 14% of 134), but the share re-addicted stays small in every figure (about 2% to 14% of men addicted in Vietnam, by sample and time frame).

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a single cohort; the three-year report (Robins et al., 1980) and the later follow-ups were not read.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive claim (proportions in one cohort): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS 6.3); not downgraded (see the domain notes): low. Strict reading: the three-year re-addiction, the treatment figures and the regular-use figure come only from the principal investigator's lecture and alone would be very low. Status single study: the 1975 report and the 1993 lecture describe one cohort and are counted once. The comparison with civilian patients at Lexington is with another study's treated population, not a control group, and is reported as the author's contrast; the matched civilian comparison group the lecture describes gives no figures here. The claim describes what happened to these men; it does not say why (the first report leaves open the men's backgrounds or the change of setting), and the treatment figures describe who entered treatment, not what treatment did. Not used: the lecture's '6% overall' (no time frame; its own figure shows about 12%), and Heyman's (2013) restatement of these figures, which joins numbers for different groups and time spans.
rate.population: US Army enlisted men (no officers, no women) who left Vietnam for the United States in September 1971, half of them under 21 on arrival in Vietnam: a random general sample of 470 (451 interviewed) and a random sample of 495 of the about 1,400 whose departure urine was positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates (898 of the 943 selected interviewed 8 to 12 months after return); about 3 years after departure, 94% of the men first interviewed were interviewed again
rate.exposure: Narcotic use (heroin or opium) and self-reported addiction in Vietnam in 1970–71, where heroin was cheap, pure, widely offered and could be smoked; addiction self-reported and checked against frequency and length of use and withdrawal symptoms (in the first report also by the study's own criteria)
rate.comparator: The same men before service and after return (no comparison group for remission); the lecture contrasts young civilian patients treated at the federal narcotics hospital in Lexington (another study)
rate.outcome: Addiction again after return, as self-reported: in the 8 to 12 months after return (first report) and in the first year and at any time in the 3 years after return (lecture); narcotic use after return; entry into drug treatment after return
rate.magnitude: Robins (1993): in Vietnam 45% tried narcotics (34% heroin, 38% opium), 20% reported addiction; of men addicted in Vietnam, addicted again in the first year after return 5%, at any time in 3 years 12% (the text also gives '6% overall', with no time frame; Figure 6 about 12%, measured by the editors); after return nearly half (text) or about 61% (Figure 6) used narcotics, about 43% heroin and about 23% regularly (Figure 6, approximate), and about half of the men who used heroin regularly were re-addicted; simple detoxification in service for a third of men addicted in Vietnam; drug treatment after return for under 2% of men who used narcotics in Vietnam, 6% of men positive at departure and 14% of those positive at departure who kept using; two-thirds of treated men relapsed by the time of interview. Robins et al. (1975), general sample N = 451, before Vietnam / in Vietnam / since return: narcotics 11% / 43% / 10%; addiction by self-report 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%; of the 196 who used narcotics in Vietnam, 46% (self-report) and 47% (criteria) addicted; 7% of the men who used narcotics after return became addicted (about 3 of 45 in the general sample, editors' calculation on the card); men first addicted in Vietnam addicted again 8 to 10 months after return about 2% (N = 90, general sample) and about 7% (N = 341, urine-positive sample), read approximately from the figure; still addicted at departure (N = 134, both samples, unweighted): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% addicted again; stated remission rate 95% (no denominator).
rate.short: Mostly not. Of US soldiers addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home, and 12 in 100 within 3 years.
rate.rate: One well-run study: nearly every man chosen was interviewed, and answers were checked. But it's one war, in unusual conditions. The 3-year figures come from the lead researcher's later lecture.

risk_of_bias.note: The online-report study (card sc_vrolijk_2017: JBI moderate) does not say how many reports were found, excluded or left without a matching tablet, how a comparison value was chosen when several tablets matched (10.8 in 100 reports), or how many scorers there were, whether they were blind and whether they agreed; its reference is a database of tablets matched by description within 12 weeks, not the tablet each report described; and 'dangerous' is defined three ways, with 'relevant' amounts never in numbers. The monitoring data (cards sc_vogels_2009 and sc_brunt_2011: JBI moderate; sc_brunt_2017: high as a measure of markets) are tablets people chose to bring in, exclude tablets identified by look, and rest their stated reliability on unpublished checks. All four papers are by, or led by, the team that runs the reference system. One level, not two: the main percentages come from a laboratory-based reference with tight intervals, and these problems could shift them but are unlikely to reverse the pattern (frequent errors, more overstatement than understatement).

inconsistency.note: One study for the accuracy of online reports; the monitoring papers agree that tablets sold as ecstasy varied widely in content from year to year, and none contradicts the online study.

indirectness.note: No study measured what the question asks: whether tablets that share a logo or look hold the same drug and amount. The online study measures how well posted descriptions matched laboratory records of tablets fitting the same description, which mixes wrong reports with look-alike tablets that differ, and the tablets the reports were about were never tested; the monitoring data describe tablets in general, not tablets that share a logo. All data are Dutch (1993–2015), where a national testing system may make online information better than elsewhere (the authors' caution).

imprecision.note: 471 reports; the main percentages have 95% intervals about 3 to 5 points either side. The look-alike statements and the monthly lows have no counts and are worded as the authors' statements; they do not carry the rating.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study and one monitoring series; the authors describe the online study as the first of its kind.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive (shares of online reports and of tablets): starts low and is never upgraded; risk of bias −1 and indirectness −1 (see the domain notes); very low. It is not rated as a test-accuracy study (METHODS 6.3): an online report is not a test, and the laboratory reference was not applied to the tablet each report described. Status single study: the accuracy of online reports rests on one study; Vogels et al. (2009), Brunt and Niesink (2011) and Brunt et al. (2017) are successive publications of the same Dutch monitoring system and team (Brunt is an author of all four papers, Niesink of three), describe other things (what tablets held; how tablets are identified by look) and do not replicate it. The answer to the question, that nobody has shown that a logo or look tells what a tablet holds, rests on the absence of a study, not on a finding against it: the Dutch system's recognition by measurements, logo and a colour test against recently analysed tablets is not shown to be unreliable either, but its reliability is unpublished (editors' reading). The 21 against 12 in 100 is an editors' reconstruction that reproduces the paper's chi-square exactly; the paper's 'approximately twice as likely' is the odds ratio. Rule 0 ('I barely felt it'): the statement names overstated reports as one possible reason someone felt little from a pill and says these studies did not look at other reasons or at what happens when people then take more; it gives no advice, and the amounts are tablet contents, not doses.
rate.population: Online reports about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market posted on Pillreports.net (218) and Partyflock.nl (253) between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2015 (471 reports; who posted them is unknown); tablets sold as ecstasy that people handed in at Dutch DIMS test offices, 33,006 of them analysed in the laboratory in 1993–2008, with the system's statements to July 2010; and the identification of tablets by look at Dutch test offices and, as described, at European drug-checking services in 2008–2013
rate.exposure: A tablet's logo and other visible features (shape, colour, size, weight): as described, with or without a picture, in online reports; and as used, with a Marquis colour test, by Dutch test-office staff to recognise tablets on a weekly updated list of tablets recently analysed in the laboratory
rate.comparator: Laboratory analysis of tablets handed in to DIMS (gas chromatography–mass spectrometry and other methods): for online reports, tablets fitting the report's description handed in within 12 weeks before or after it, not the tablet the report described; no study compared tablets that share a logo with each other, and the validation data for recognition by look are unpublished
rate.outcome: Share of online reports whose stated MDMA amount was more than 10 mg above or below (or more than 40 mg below) the laboratory value for matching tablets, that left out substances found in them, or that the authors scored as 'dangerous'; share whose description fitted more than one distinct tablet; report features (picture, range of amounts) associated with 'dangerous' reports; look-alike tablets holding other drugs (no counts); share of tablets identified by look and its stated reliability; content of laboratory-analysed tablets sold as ecstasy by year (share with only MDMA; MDMA per tablet)
rate.magnitude: Vrolijk et al. (2017): 471 online reports (Pillreports.net 218, Partyflock.nl 253), 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2015, each compared with DIMS laboratory records (GC–MS) of tablets fitting its description handed in within 12 weeks before or after it; percentages with 95% bootstrap CIs (1,000 samples; Table 1): MDMA stated more than 10 mg too high 39.7% (35.2–44.4; Pillreports 47.7, Partyflock 32.8; χ² 10.86, P = 0.001); more than 10 mg too low 17.6% (14.0–21.2); more than 40 mg too low 10.2% (7.6–13.0); unreported substance 15.5% (12.3–18.9); unreported substance scored dangerous 7.0% (4.7–9.3); 'dangerous' overall 15.3% (11.9–18.5); mean difference 10.6 mg too high (6.7–14.4); within 10 mg or no amount given: not reported, at most 42.7% (editors' calculation, 100 − 39.7 − 17.6). Multiple database hits 10.8% (8.1–13.6); picture included 46.9% (42.3–51.2); picture with multiple hits Exp(b) 0.298 (0.111–0.799), P = 0.016; multiple hits with more than 40 mg too low 4.880 (1.608–14.81), P = 0.005, and with an unreported substance 2.556 (1.056–6.186), P = 0.037; multiple hits with 'dangerous' χ² 34.26, P < 0.001; picture with 'dangerous' 1.044 (0.490–2.225), P = 0.912. Range given in 66.2% (61.8–70.1); range with 'dangerous' Exp(b) 0.511 (0.307–0.850), P = 0.010; Pearson χ² 6.890 (printed P 0.007). Editors' reconstruction from Table 1 and the site totals (range 148 + 164 = 312, none 159; 'dangerous' 32 + 40 = 72; data/verification/pdf-2026-11-26/754_calculations.py): 'dangerous' in 34 of 159 reports without a range (21.4%) and 38 of 312 with one (12.2%), the only split that gives Pearson χ² 6.890; ratio of proportions about 1.76, odds ratio about 1.96 (= 1/0.511), the paper's 'approximately twice as likely'. Vogels et al. (2009): 33,006 laboratory-analysed tablets sold as ecstasy, 1993–2008; only MDMA as active substance 44% (1997) to 86% on average (2000–2004); median MDMA per tablet 73 mg over the period, yearly 60 mg (1998) to 84 mg (1994); single tablets from under 1 mg (traces) to 225 mg (tablet contents, not doses). Identification by look and a Marquis test against a weekly list: on average 30% of tablets; reliability stated as 99% from internal checks, without data (Vogels et al., 2009; Brunt & Niesink, 2011); called very reliable in the Netherlands, citing those two papers (Brunt et al., 2017). Brunt & Niesink (2011): tablets with MDMA or an MDMA-like substance 30% in October 1997 and tablets with MDMA 40% in March 2009 (monthly lows, no denominators); 2C-B in tablets resembling ecstasy, with similar logos, shapes and colours, in the second half of the 2000s, and amphetamine in tablets with logos similar to ecstasy (no counts). No paper reports how content varied among tablets sharing a logo.
rate.short: Nobody has shown it can. In a Dutch check, about 40 in 100 online pill reports claimed over 10 mg more MDMA than lab tests found in matching pills.
rate.rate: One Dutch study of two websites, by the team that runs the lab records it checked against. Nobody measured how much pills with the same logo differ, and the '99% reliable' figure has no published data.

risk_of_bias.note: The claim is about which people choose benzodiazepines, a comparison between kinds of people. The contrast between people with and without histories of problem drug use is made across separate studies, by different laboratories, mostly at very different doses and with different procedures, so dose and procedure could explain it; the review reports that choice depended on dose but does not discuss this. The review's selection is unsystematic (card sc_griffiths_1997: high), 11 of its 13 drug-history studies are the first author's, and several of its labels rest on its own one-tailed re-tests. Within de Wit et al. (1986) anxious and non-anxious volunteers were compared at the same doses (RoB 2 some concerns on card sc_de_wit_1986: allocation to orders not described, staff blinding not stated, completers only, mood results tabulated only where significant).

inconsistency.note: Within each kind of person the direction is consistent: volunteers without problem drug use did not choose a benzodiazepine over placebo in any of the single-dose or capsule-by-capsule studies tabulated for them, and people with problem drug use chose it in every placebo-controlled study tabulated for them. The mixed results in anxious people and in insomnia line up with the procedure (a single morning dose against capsules as needed, or a forced choice against optional use), an explanation the review offers, untested, and the statement gives.

indirectness.note: Apart from de Wit et al. (1986), the evidence is second-hand, through one narrative review whose primary papers were not read. All the studies are laboratory or clinic studies from 1976 to 1997, mostly with single doses or single sessions of capsules prepared by the researchers, small samples and, among people with problem drug use, almost only men; what they show about choosing benzodiazepines outside a laboratory is not known.

imprecision.note: 2 to 16 people per study among people with problem drug use and about 10 to 14 per group in most other studies; the comparisons between kinds of people are small (de Wit et al.: 11 to 13 per group, no difference detected; anxious against other volunteers 65% against 45%, P = 0.06; moderate against light drinkers significant in one study of 27 people); no pooled estimate or interval.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a narrative review; the review does tabulate negative human studies, though not every negative animal study.

rate.reasoning: Rated as observational because the claim is about who chooses benzodiazepines, a comparison between kinds of people made mostly across separate studies (METHODS 6.3; brief for this round), although each study's own comparison of the drug with a placebo is within-person and mostly double-blind. Low start; risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 give very low (the scale stops there). The within-person finding of de Wit et al. (1986) alone, that 36 volunteers without problem drug use, anxious or not, mostly chose a placebo over single morning doses of diazepam, which calmed and sedated them without raising euphoria scores, rests on a counterbalanced, placebo-controlled comparison and a behavioural outcome and would be moderate on its own (high start; imprecision −1: 36 people, no intervals); the same laboratory found the same in other volunteers, as the review summarizes, which is replication by the same team. The contrast with people with problem drug use rests on the review's comparison of separate studies by another laboratory, mostly at much higher doses, and cannot separate history from dose; the statement says so and does not give it as the review's own caution, which it is not. Status replicated by the same team: volunteers without problem drug use were studied mainly by the Chicago group (de Wit, Johanson, Uhlenhuth) and people with problem drug use mainly by the review's first author's group, and no study read compared the two at the same doses. Choosing a drug over a placebo is not the same as feeling high: the review's definition of reinforcement covers any motive, and only de Wit et al. measured euphoria directly. The school-survey figure is second-hand and the national survey figure qualifies the claim without being part of the rating. The review's findings on how fast the drug acts and its comparisons of benzodiazepines by appeal are left out by design. Doses are given only as study conditions; nothing here is advice on amounts or use.
rate.population: Adults in laboratory choice studies: in the primary study read, 36 paid volunteers aged 21 to 35 at the University of Chicago without a history of problem drug use (12 without anxiety, 11 with anxious mood and 13 with DSM-III generalized anxiety disorder; 22 women); as summarized second-hand by a narrative review of studies published up to 1997, people with histories of problem drug use (13 studies of 2 to 16 people, men in all but one) and people without (17 studies: healthy volunteers, light and moderate social drinkers, people with or without an alcoholic first-degree relative, anxious people, people with insomnia); for context, US adults reporting benzodiazepine misuse in a 2015–2016 national survey
rate.exposure: A benzodiazepine given by the researchers by mouth, mostly double-blind, in capsules of a colour that people learned during sampling sessions (study conditions: in the primary study single morning doses of 5 or 10 mg diazepam on separate days; in the review's studies diazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam, oxazepam, triazolam or flurazepam, mostly at much higher doses in people with histories of problem drug use, for example diazepam 40 to 400 mg in three studies, and diazepam in single doses of 2 to 20 mg or in 4 mg capsules taken one at a time in others)
rate.comparator: Placebo capsules in the same people (a choice between the two colours, or self-administration of each); kinds of people compared across separate studies (problem drug use or not) and within some studies (anxious or not; moderate or light drinkers); d,l-amphetamine 5 mg as a comparison drug in the primary study
rate.outcome: How often the benzodiazepine was chosen or taken rather than placebo; liking ratings; identification of the capsule; mood questionnaires (Profile of Mood States; the ARCI questionnaire with euphoria, sedation and dysphoria scales); for context, the main reason for misuse people gave in a national survey
rate.magnitude: de Wit et al. (1986), 36 people (controls 12, anxious mood 11, generalized anxiety disorder 13), numbers choosing the drug on 0–1, 2–3 and 4–5 of 5 choice sessions: diazepam 5 mg 21, 7, 8 (trend z = −2.2, P < .03); diazepam 10 mg 27, 4, 5 (controls 9, 1, 2; anxious mood 10, 1, 0; generalized anxiety 8, 2, 3; z = −3.0, P < .004); d,l-amphetamine 5 mg 6, 10, 20 (z = 2.3, P < .02); no group differences. Editors' shares: diazepam at most once 58 in 100 (5 mg) and 75 in 100 (10 mg), four or five times 22 and 14 in 100; amphetamine four or five times 56 in 100. Mean amphetamine choices 4.0, 3.1 and 2.9 of 5 (controls, anxious mood, generalized anxiety), about 67% overall (editors' calculation from the printed means; the review's Table 3 estimates 73%). Liking over the sampling sessions (Table 5; equal ratings left out): placebo liked more by 17 and diazepam by 8 at 5 mg (11 equal); by 21 and 9 at 10 mg (5 equal; 35 of the 36 accounted for); choice by liking z = 2.51 (P < .02) at 5 mg; at 10 mg placebo chosen more whichever capsule was liked more, z = 2.63 (P < .01). Identification: 10 mg diazepam called a tranquilizer by 30 of 36, 5 mg by 18 of 32. Mood (Table 6): both doses lowered Anxiety, Vigor, Arousal and the stimulant-like BG scale and raised Confusion and the sedation (PCAG) scale (drug by hour, P = .001 to .04); 10 mg raised Fatigue (P = .001), Depression (P = .03) and the dysphoria (LSD) scale (P = .01) and lowered Friendliness (P = .004), Elation (P = .003) and Positive Mood (P = .003); no significant diazepam effect on the euphoria (MBG) scale; amphetamine on MBG drug by hour P = .001. Background (Table 2; editors' sums): marijuana ever 29, stimulants ever 19, tranquilizers outside medical care ever 6, more than 7 drinks a week 9, of 36. Griffiths & Weerts (1997), as tabulated (second-hand): people with histories of problem drug use, 13 studies, 2 to 16 people each; diazepam chosen over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% (16 men); lorazepam chosen over buspirone by 7 of 8; triazolam a reinforcer in 4 of 6, and chosen before relaxation by 8 of 8 and before a vigilance task by 0 of 8; 4 of 13 studies without a placebo comparison (editors' count). People without such histories, 17 studies: diazepam 28% and 27% of choice sessions (5 and 10 mg; 10 people), 25%, 32% and 38% (three groups), 28% (estimated, de Wit et al., 1986), 33% (43 people); lorazepam 2 mg 16% and flurazepam 30 mg 20% (12 people each); 5 mg d-amphetamine 76%. Moderate against light social drinkers (about 12 against 4 drinks a week): 100% against 66% (12 and 18 people), 73% against 40% (14 and 13; difference significant); moderate drinkers 64% diazepam (30 people) against 27% buspirone (25 others). Anxious people: 37% (14 seeking treatment, single morning dose); 65% against 45% (22 and 23 people; P = 0.06); 3 of 4; 11 of 14. Insomnia: triazolam on 86% of nights under forced choice (three groups of 8); capsules on 77% (triazolam) and 80% (placebo) of nights when only one was available. As cited: about half of US high-school students reporting non-medical tranquilizer use usually got high. Maust et al. (2019): main reason for benzodiazepine misuse to get high 11.6% (13.9% at ages 18–49, 3.0% at 50 or older), against relaxing 47.1% and sleep 26.6%.
rate.short: Depends who you are. In one lab study, 27 of 36 people without drug problems mostly chose a dummy pill over Valium. People with past drug problems almost always chose benzos.
rate.rate: Small, old lab studies. The one read in full was careful, but the comparison between kinds of people comes second-hand from a review of separate studies that used very different doses.

risk_of_bias.note: Australian series (card sc_ryan_2015: JBI, moderate): every admission to one unit, recorded prospectively by staff blinded to this study, but amounts and drugs were taken from patients' and others' accounts without laboratory confirmation, 41 of 112 admissions were left out (16 for an unknown amount, 3 of whom had seizures), tachycardia and the way seizures were ascertained are not defined, and nothing is adjusted for the other medicines most people took. Iranian review (card sc_rostam_abadi_2020: AMSTAR 2, critically low): no protocol, publication bias not considered, risk of bias not carried into the interpretation; the primary series were not appraised for laboratory confirmation, some may share patients, and some may have drawn patients selected for seizures. These problems could change the frequencies materially.

inconsistency.note: Seizures in 11 in 100 Australian admissions (and 8 and 14 in two earlier series the authors cite) against a pooled 34.6 in Iranian series that themselves range from about 12 to 69 in 100 (I² 94%; prediction interval 12.5 to 60.9); deaths from 0 to 10 in 100 between Iranian series (I² 92%), two from the same city and years giving 10 and 0.9. The suggested reasons (selection in Tehran, enzyme differences in Iran) were not tested. The statement gives the ranges, but no single frequency can be given with confidence.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the claim describes people admitted to hospital after an overdose and says that it gives no risk for people taking tramadol, for people who did not reach hospital or for ordinary amounts; the bound on serotonin toxicity is stated for such overdoses only.

imprecision.note: The Australian frequencies rest on few events (8 seizures and 13 people with respiratory depression; exact 95% intervals 5 to 21 and 10 to 29 in 100) and serotonin toxicity on none in 71 (upper limit 5.1 in 100), all given in the statement; the spread of the Iranian figures is counted under inconsistency. Not downgraded again.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; series of hospital admissions are reported whatever their frequencies, which do not depend on a significant result.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive (frequencies among hospital admissions after a tramadol overdose): starts low; down one level for risk of bias and one for inconsistency; very low; never upgraded (descriptive claims are not). Status replicated: seizures in a substantial share of admissions were found independently in the Australian series and in the Iranian series (counted once, as one review), in the same direction but at very different frequencies. The figures for consciousness, respiratory depression, naloxone and the absence of serotonin toxicity rest on the Australian series alone (single study); the Iranian breathing data are listed for only five series, as one of each series' three commonest other features. The pooled Iranian death figure (0.7 in 100) gives the series similar weights; most of the deaths in the pooled series come from one series of 1,023 with 10 in 100 (editors' approximation from Figure 6). Seizures at ordinary amounts were not measured in any study read: the adverse-reaction reports and the case report show only that such seizures were reported. The sentence on feeling little rests on background statements both papers cite, not on their own measurements.
rate.population: People admitted to hospital after a tramadol overdose: 71 admissions (70 people) after more than 400 mg at one Australian toxicology unit, November 2000 to June 2013; Iranian hospital and poison-centre series of people admitted with tramadol poisoning, mostly 2004–2017 and mostly young men (23 series, 5,972 admissions, for seizures; 18 series, 4,761, for deaths); and, for seizures outside an overdose, Iranian adverse-reaction reports and one case report
rate.exposure: Tramadol overdose (in the Australian series more than 400 mg, median reported 1,000 mg, with other medicines in 51 of 71); in the Iranian series tramadol poisoning, taken alone by 43 to 100 in 100 where reported
rate.comparator: None outside the series (no comparison with other overdoses or with people taking tramadol without an overdose); within the Australian series, admissions after tramadol alone against those with other medicines, and reported amounts with and without seizures or respiratory depression
rate.outcome: Seizures; reduced consciousness and coma (Glasgow Coma Scale below 15 and below 9); respiratory depression (oxygen saturation below 94%); serotonin toxicity (Hunter criteria); intensive care; death in hospital; in Iran, also tramadol's share of seizure presentations
rate.magnitude: Ryan & Isbister (2015), 71 admissions after more than 400 mg (median reported 1,000 mg, IQR 800–2,000, range 450–6,000; slow-release in 22), 51 with other medicines (benzodiazepine 16, SSRI 13, SNRI 10, tricyclic 3; Table 1): seizures 8/71 (11%; exact 95% CI 5.0–21.0, editors' calculation); tramadol only 2/20 (10%) against with other medicines 6/51 (12%) (Table 2); reported amount with against without seizures median 2,100 (IQR 1,600–3,250) against 1,000 mg (775–1,550), p = 0.018 (text) or 0.021 (Figure 1); first seizure median 8.5 h (1.5–22.7), immediate-release 1.5–11 h, slow-release 6.5–22.7 h; seizures also in 3 of 16 admissions excluded for an unknown amount. Glasgow Coma Scale below 15: 29/71 (41%; 29.3–53.2); below 9: 5/71 (7%; 2.3–15.7), 3 after tricyclics. Respiratory depression (oxygen saturation below 94%): 13/71 (18%; 10.1–29.3, editors' calculation), onset 2 h or less in 7 of 9 with a known time; reported amount 2,500 (1,600–3,000) against 1,000 mg (750–1,475), p = 0.003; 5 of 13 with a tricyclic, promethazine or pneumonia (Figure 4). Tachycardia 27 (38%); systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg 32 (45%); vomiting or nausea 36 (51%). Naloxone given to 9: improved 6, partly 2, not 1. Intensive care 8 (all after co-ingestion: 5 co-ingestant toxicity, 3 respiratory depression); deaths 0/71 (0–5.1%). Hunter serotonin toxicity 0/71 (exact 95% upper limit 5.1%, editors' calculation; one-sided 95% upper limit 4.1%). Rostam-Abadi et al. (2020), Iranian admissions with tramadol poisoning: seizures pooled 34.6% (95% CI 29.6–39.8), I² 94.0%, 23 series (5,972 admissions, editors' sum of the sample sizes in Figure 5), single series 11.7–69.3% (12.0–69.3% in the text), prediction interval 12.5–60.9% (Figure 5); deaths pooled 0.7% (0.0–1.9), I² 91.7%, 18 series (4,761 admissions, editors' sum from Figure 6), prediction interval 0–10.0%, six series with none, the highest 10.0% (Kermanshah, 1,023) against 0.9% (Kermanshah, 546, overlapping years); by the editors' approximation from the rounded proportions in Figure 6, about 129 deaths in all, about 102 of them in the 10.0% series. Table 5: apnoea 4.7%, 3.6%, 6.2% and 15.0% (20 children) in the four series that list it; bradypnoea 18.0% in one; tramadol alone in 43.0–100% of cases where reported. Table 4: tramadol poisoning in 21.9% of 383 first seizures, 36.8% of 141 seizures, 39.5% of 143 and 54.7% of 137 drug-induced seizures. National adverse-reaction reports, 2006–10: 249 people, seizure the most reported reaction (29.3% in the text, 29.5% in Table 5). One case report: seizure after 200 mg by mouth, no other drug (Table 6).
rate.short: In overdoses, seizures are common. 11 in 100 people treated at one Australian unit had them, and about 35 in 100 in Iran. Some had trouble breathing too.

inconsistency.note: Where the same medicine was tested on several assays, results differed by assay, which the statement gives as the rule rather than a contradiction; the reviews disagree on one test (efavirenz and the Drug Screen Multi 5), which the statement reports.

indirectness.note: Second-hand. imprecision.note: The few frequencies come from single chart reviews of 26 to 53 linked results with their totals unprinted, from groups of 6, 30 or 50 people, or from percentages without denominators.

item.statement: Most Vietnam veterans who got over heroin addiction did it through treatment.
item.why: Fewer than 2 in 100 men who'd used narcotics in Vietnam entered drug treatment back home, and those who did relapsed as often as civilian patients.

lines.short: Mostly not. Of US soldiers addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home, and 12 in 100 within 3 years.
lines.but: Vietnam was unusual: heroin was cheap, pure and everywhere. The lead researcher says few of these young men would have become addicted at home.
how: In Vietnam in 1970–71, almost half of US Army enlisted men tried narcotics, mostly heroin or opium. 20 in 100 said they'd been addicted there.
Back home, many used again without getting addicted again. Even among men who used heroin often, only about half got addicted again.
Treatment wasn't the reason, the lead researcher says. Fewer than 2 in 100 men who'd used narcotics in Vietnam entered drug treatment back home. Those who did relapsed as often as civilian patients.
These are the men's own reports, checked against military records and urine tests. The 3-year figures come from the lead researcher's later lecture, whose text and graphs don't always match.

item.statement: An online pill report with a photo is more likely to be right.
item.why: In a Dutch check against lab tests, a photo helped match a report to the right pill. But reports with photos were not less often dangerously wrong: far too little MDMA, or a drug left out.

lines.short: Nobody has shown it can. In a Dutch check, about 40 in 100 online pill reports claimed over 10 mg more MDMA than lab tests found in matching pills.
lines.but: Nobody has measured how much pills with the same logo differ. And the online check is one Dutch study of two websites.
how: Staff of the Dutch testing service compared 471 online reports about ecstasy pills from 2014–15 with lab results for pills matching each description. About 40 in 100 said over 10 mg too much MDMA, 18 in 100 over 10 mg too little, and 16 in 100 missed another drug.

The authors called 15 in 100 reports dangerous: far too little MDMA, or a drug left out. Saying too much wasn't counted. A photo helped find the right pill but didn't make reports less often dangerous. Reports giving a range were dangerous less often: 12 against 21 in 100.

The same testers say pills that looked like ecstasy, with similar logos, have held 2C-B or amphetamine. They identify some pills by exact size, weight, logo and a colour test, against pills tested in recent weeks. They call it 99% reliable but have published no data.

In lab tests of Dutch pills sold as ecstasy from 1993 to 2008, only MDMA was found in 44 in 100 in 1997 and about 86 in 100 in 2000–04. Single pills held from a trace to 225 mg. These are lab amounts, not amounts to take.

item.statement: Most people would pick Valium over a dummy pill.
item.why: In a lab study, most young volunteers without drug problems chose the dummy pill. It was one small study, and people with a history of drug problems did choose benzos in other studies.

lines.short: Depends who you are. In one lab study, 27 of 36 people without drug problems mostly chose a dummy pill over Valium. People with past drug problems almost always chose benzos.
lines.but: But those people were tested in other labs' studies, mostly with much bigger doses. So we can't tell if their past made the difference.
how: In a 1980s study, 36 young volunteers with no history of drug problems (most had tried cannabis) tried Valium and a dummy pill, then chose between them five times. Most picked the dummy pill, anxious or not.
Valium calmed them and made them sleepy and a bit muddled. It didn't raise their scores for euphoria. At the higher dose they felt more tired and less cheerful than on the dummy pill.

A review of older lab studies found that people with a history of drug problems almost always chose benzos. Moderate drinkers chose Valium more than light drinkers did. Anxious people chose benzos when they could take them as needed.

Outside the lab, some people say they get high. A review cites an older US school survey in which about half of teens who took calming pills without a prescription said they usually got high. In a newer adult survey, 12 in 100 who misused benzos said getting high was their main reason.

item.statement: With too much tramadol, seizures only happen if other drugs were taken too.
item.why: In one Australian study, 2 of 20 people who took only tramadol had seizures, against 6 of 51 who took other pills too. These were overdoses, not normal doses.

lines.but: These were overdoses, often with other pills too. No one checked the risk at normal doses.
how: At one Australian hospital unit, 8 of 71 people treated for a tramadol overdose had seizures. That was 2 of the 20 who took only tramadol, and 6 of the 51 who took other pills too. Some came almost a day later.

18 in 100 had breathing trouble with low oxygen, and 5 went into a coma (3 of them had also taken an older type of antidepressant). Those who said they took more had more seizures and breathing trouble. Nobody died.

In 23 Iranian hospital studies, about 35 in 100 had seizures, but single studies ranged from 12 to 69 in 100. About 7 in 1,000 died in hospital; one study had 100 in 1,000.

item.statement: A positive drug screen always means the person took that drug.
item.why: Screens use antibodies that can react to some medicines, like efavirenz on one benzo test. Most reports are single cases. Both reviews say a different lab method should check a screen.

lines.short: Yes, some can, on certain tests. On one benzo test, 46 of 50 people taking the HIV drug efavirenz screened positive, but a lab check found no benzos.
lines.but: Most reports describe one or a few people, or a medicine added to urine in a lab. No one has counted how often it happens to people who take them.
how: Quick screens use antibodies, which can grab molecules that look alike. Reviews name sertraline for benzo tests. They name bupropion and pseudoephedrine for amphetamine tests, and some antibiotics for opiate tests.
Only a few numbers exist. In two chart reviews, 41 in 100 unconfirmed amphetamine screens came from people taking bupropion, and about 27 in 100 false benzo screens were linked to sertraline.

Some medicines give true positives, because they are or become the drug tested. Examples: prescribed amphetamines, prescribed THC, and codeine, which turns into morphine. There is no evidence that amoxicillin trips a cocaine test. Numbing drugs like lidocaine do not.
Both reviews say a screen is only a first step. A different lab method should check it before a big decision, like a job or a court case.

item.statement: Death rates were about the same in and out of methadone treatment.
item.why: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. People who leave differ in other ways, so this can't show cause.

lines.short: Deaths were more common off treatment, most of all in the first 4 weeks after leaving. In 16 methadone studies, about 36 in 1,000 died a year off treatment, against 11 on it.
lines.but: The main figures lump together everyone who left, for any reason. People who leave differ in other ways. So the studies can't show that stopping itself caused the deaths.
how: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. Every group had more deaths out of treatment, though in the biggest recent groups the gap was smaller: about 6 or 7 a year, against 12 to 18.

5 recent studies, with lower death rates overall, split deaths by time: about 32 a year per 1,000 people in the first 4 weeks off methadone, against about 14 later on. The first 4 weeks on it looked riskier too, but that could be chance.

With buprenorphine, almost all the deaths came from Australian studies. Deaths were also higher in the first 4 weeks off, about 32 against 11 a year per 1,000, but that's from just two studies. Counting overdoses alone, 3 methadone studies found no clear rise in those weeks, but only 20 happened then.

Did finishing treatment matter? Only 3 studies looked, and the review doesn't say what finishing meant. In two small ones, deaths after leaving ran 3 to 4 times higher when treatment wasn't finished (about 69 against 17, and 84 against 26 a year per 1,000). The third, which counted only the first 4 weeks, found no clear difference.
