how: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. Every group had more deaths out of treatment, though in the biggest recent groups the gap was smaller: about 6 or 7 a year, against 12 to 18.

5 recent studies, with lower death rates overall, split deaths by time: about 32 a year per 1,000 people in the first 4 weeks off methadone, against about 14 later on. The first 4 weeks on it looked riskier too, but that could be chance.

With buprenorphine, almost all the deaths came from Australian studies. Deaths were also higher in the first 4 weeks off, about 32 against 11 a year per 1,000, but that's from just two studies. Counting overdoses alone, 3 methadone studies found no clear rise in those weeks, but only 20 happened then.

Did finishing treatment matter? Only 3 studies looked, and the review doesn't say what finishing meant. In two small ones, deaths after leaving ran 3 to 4 times higher when treatment wasn't finished (about 69 against 17, and 84 against 26 a year per 1,000). The third, which counted only the first 4 weeks, found no clear difference.

lines.statement: Among US Army enlisted men who served in Vietnam in 1970–1971, narcotic use and self-reported addiction were common, but few of the men addicted there were addicted again after they came home, and by the principal investigator's account treatment did not explain this; she also says that the conditions in Vietnam were unlike anything before. In her later account, 45% of Army enlisted men in Vietnam in 1970–71 tried narcotics (34% heroin, 38% opium) and 20% said they had felt strung out or addicted there, claims the researchers accepted after asking about frequency and length of use and about withdrawal symptoms; heroin there was cheap, pure and did not have to be injected, more than 80% of men were offered it, usually within a week of arrival, and those who became addicted had typically begun early in their tour, before exposure to combat (Robins, 1993). In the study's first report, of 451 men interviewed from a random sample of 470 who left Vietnam in September 1971, 43% had used narcotics there; of these 196 men, 46% said they had been addicted (47% by the study's own criteria: at least three of more-than-weekly use for over a month, two or more of four withdrawal symptoms, withdrawal lasting at least two days or 12 hours if eased, and believing oneself addicted), which is 20% of all the men (21% by the criteria), against 0.2% (0.4%) before Vietnam and 0.7% (1%) in the 8 to 12 months after return, when 10% had used a narcotic (Robins et al., 1975). Of the men addicted in Vietnam, 5% were addicted in the first year after return and 12% at any time in the 3 years after return, usually briefly (Robins, 1993); the first report's figure, read approximately, shows about 2% of 90 such men in the random sample and about 7% of 341 in a second sample, selected on a positive urine test at departure, addicted 8 to 10 months after return, and how the 5% combines the samples is not stated. The lecture's text also gives '6% overall' re-addicted, without a time frame, but its own Figure 6 shows about 12%, matching the three-year figure, which is the one used here. Many men used narcotics again without becoming addicted again: nearly half of those addicted in Vietnam tried narcotics again after return, by the text (about 6 in 10 in Figure 6, read approximately), and of those who used heroin regularly about half were re-addicted (Robins, 1993); of 134 men still addicted when they left Vietnam (both samples, unweighted), 50% used a narcotic in the months after return and 14% were addicted again; and the first report gives 7% of the men who used narcotics after return becoming addicted, against about half of those who used them in Vietnam (Robins et al., 1975; in the random sample about 3 of some 45 men, editors' calculation on the study card). A third of the men addicted in Vietnam received even simple detoxification in service, and after return fewer than 2% of the men who had used narcotics in Vietnam, 6% of men positive at departure and 14% of those positive at departure who kept using entered drug treatment; men who did enter treatment relapsed as often as young civilians treated at the federal narcotics hospital in Lexington, two-thirds by the time of interview, and the principal investigator reads treated cases as people who cannot stop on their own; and among the men who used narcotics again, none of the factors tested predicted who became addicted again, including behaviour problems before service, which had predicted narcotic use in Vietnam, parents' problems, drug use in Vietnam, IQ, combat and demographic characteristics (Robins, 1993). The men were young enlisted soldiers from one month's departures, in a setting where, she writes, never before had so many young men been addicted to opiates without the usual risk factors and where few of them would have become addicted had they stayed in the US; addiction was self-reported, checked against military records (97% of men whose records showed narcotic use reported it) and urine taken at interview; the lecture gives no total sample size, no definition of re-addiction and no intervals, several of its text figures differ from its graphs, and its three-year figures could not be checked against the three-year report, which was not read; and the first report leaves open whether the men's backgrounds or the change of setting explains the recovery. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: US Army enlisted men (no officers, no women) who left Vietnam for the United States in September 1971, half of them under 21 on arrival in Vietnam: a random general sample of 470 (451 interviewed) and a random sample of 495 of the about 1,400 whose departure urine was positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates (898 of the 943 selected interviewed 8 to 12 months after return); about 3 years after departure, 94% of the men first interviewed were interviewed again
lines.exposure: Narcotic use (heroin or opium) and self-reported addiction in Vietnam in 1970–71, where heroin was cheap, pure, widely offered and could be smoked; addiction self-reported and checked against frequency and length of use and withdrawal symptoms (in the first report also by the study's own criteria)
lines.comparator: The same men before service and after return (no comparison group for remission); the lecture contrasts young civilian patients treated at the federal narcotics hospital in Lexington (another study)
lines.outcome: Addiction again after return, as self-reported: in the 8 to 12 months after return (first report) and in the first year and at any time in the 3 years after return (lecture); narcotic use after return; entry into drug treatment after return
lines.magnitude: Robins (1993): in Vietnam 45% tried narcotics (34% heroin, 38% opium), 20% reported addiction; of men addicted in Vietnam, addicted again in the first year after return 5%, at any time in 3 years 12% (the text also gives '6% overall', with no time frame; Figure 6 about 12%, measured by the editors); after return nearly half (text) or about 61% (Figure 6) used narcotics, about 43% heroin and about 23% regularly (Figure 6, approximate), and about half of the men who used heroin regularly were re-addicted; simple detoxification in service for a third of men addicted in Vietnam; drug treatment after return for under 2% of men who used narcotics in Vietnam, 6% of men positive at departure and 14% of those positive at departure who kept using; two-thirds of treated men relapsed by the time of interview. Robins et al. (1975), general sample N = 451, before Vietnam / in Vietnam / since return: narcotics 11% / 43% / 10%; addiction by self-report 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%; of the 196 who used narcotics in Vietnam, 46% (self-report) and 47% (criteria) addicted; 7% of the men who used narcotics after return became addicted (about 3 of 45 in the general sample, editors' calculation on the card); men first addicted in Vietnam addicted again 8 to 10 months after return about 2% (N = 90, general sample) and about 7% (N = 341, urine-positive sample), read approximately from the figure; still addicted at departure (N = 134, both samples, unweighted): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% addicted again; stated remission rate 95% (no denominator).
lines.reasoning: Descriptive claim (proportions in one cohort): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS 6.3); not downgraded (see the domain notes): low. Strict reading: the three-year re-addiction, the treatment figures and the regular-use figure come only from the principal investigator's lecture and alone would be very low. Status single study: the 1975 report and the 1993 lecture describe one cohort and are counted once. The comparison with civilian patients at Lexington is with another study's treated population, not a control group, and is reported as the author's contrast; the matched civilian comparison group the lecture describes gives no figures here. The claim describes what happened to these men; it does not say why (the first report leaves open the men's backgrounds or the change of setting), and the treatment figures describe who entered treatment, not what treatment did. Not used: the lecture's '6% overall' (no time frame; its own figure shows about 12%), and Heyman's (2013) restatement of these figures, which joins numbers for different groups and time spans.

lines.q: Did the soldiers addicted to heroin in Vietnam stay addicted?
lines.short: Mostly not. Of US soldiers addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home, and 12 in 100 within 3 years.
lines.but: Vietnam was unusual: heroin was cheap, pure and everywhere. The lead researcher says few of these young men would have become addicted at home.
how: In Vietnam in 1970–71, almost half of US Army enlisted men tried narcotics, mostly heroin or opium. 20 in 100 said they'd been addicted there.
Back home, many used again without getting addicted again. Even among men who used heroin often, only about half got addicted again.
Treatment wasn't the reason, the lead researcher says. Fewer than 2 in 100 men who'd used narcotics in Vietnam entered drug treatment back home. Those who did relapsed as often as civilian patients.
These are the men's own reports, checked against military records and urine tests. The 3-year figures come from the lead researcher's later lecture, whose text and graphs don't always match.

lines.statement: Whether a tablet's logo or look tells what it holds has not been measured directly in the studies read: none compared the contents of tablets that share a logo, and the 99% reliability that the Dutch Drug Information and Monitoring System (DIMS) states for identifying tablets by their look is given without data. The nearest evidence comes from the Netherlands. DIMS staff compared 471 online reports about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market, posted on Pillreports.net (218) and Partyflock.nl (253) between January 2014 and December 2015, each with the laboratory results (gas chromatography–mass spectrometry) of tablets fitting its description that had been handed in at Dutch test offices within 12 weeks before or after it. 39.7 in 100 reports (95% CI 35.2 to 44.4) stated an amount of MDMA more than 10 mg above the laboratory value and 17.6 in 100 (14.0 to 21.2) more than 10 mg below it, so that stated amounts were on average 10.6 mg too high (6.7 to 14.4); 15.5 in 100 (12.3 to 18.9) left out a substance that matching tablets contained. How many reports were within 10 mg is not given (at most 42.7 in 100, editors' calculation by subtraction). The authors scored 15.3 in 100 (11.9 to 18.5) as 'dangerous': the amount stated more than 40 mg too low (10.2 in 100), or a psychoactive substance left out in amounts they call relevant without defining them in numbers (7.0 in 100). Stating too much MDMA, the commonest error, was not scored as dangerous: the authors considered it and judged its risk too speculative. In 10.8 in 100 reports the description fitted more than one distinct tablet in the database, which the authors take to mean that several different pills on the market fitted it; reports with a picture fitted more than one tablet less often (odds ratio 0.298, 0.111 to 0.799) but were not less often 'dangerous' (1.044, 0.490 to 2.225). Reports that gave a range of amounts instead of one figure were 'dangerous' less often: 38 of 312 (12.2 in 100) against 34 of 159 without a range (21.4 in 100), an editors' reconstruction from the printed percentages and site totals that reproduces the paper's chi-square of 6.890. The paper calls reports without a range 'approximately twice as likely' to be dangerous; that is the odds ratio (1/0.511, about 1.96), while one proportion is about 1.76 times the other (editors' calculation). The authors suggest, without testing it, that pills that look alike can come from different batches or makers, with different amounts or even different substances, and that people may post amounts guessed from their own experience, or sellers post high ones to advertise; reports that named DIMS laboratory tests as their source often gave amounts that were not in its database (no count given), and reports often named no source at all (Vrolijk et al., 2017). Because each report was compared with tablets of matching description rather than with the tablet it was about, a mismatch may come from a wrong report or from a look-alike tablet with other contents, and the study cannot tell these apart (editors' reading). Some people feel little from a pill that a report called strong: reports stating too much MDMA, the commonest error here, fit one possible reason, but these studies did not look at other reasons, such as tolerance, or at what happens when people then take more. The system's own authors report, without counts, that in the second half of the 2000s tablets sold as ecstasy often held 2C-B instead, and that these highly resembled ecstasy tablets, with similar logos, shapes and colours; amphetamine, too, turns up in tablets with logos like those of ecstasy (Brunt & Niesink, 2011). At most Dutch test offices, staff identify some tablets on the spot: they record the logo, shape, colour, weight, diameter (matched to within 0.10 mm) and thickness (within 0.30 mm), do a Marquis colour test, and look for a match on a list, updated weekly, of tablets recently analysed in the laboratory; a recognised tablet is given its batch's average MDMA content without a new analysis, and tablets not recognised, or in doubt, go to the laboratory. On average 30 in 100 tablets were identified this way. The papers say that a recognised tablet's average content (and, in one, its variation) is then known, but report neither, and that checks of recognised tablets that people still had analysed showed 99% reliability, without numbers, period or what counted as right (the main substance or the amount) (Vogels et al., 2009; Brunt & Niesink, 2011); a later report from seven European drug-checking services calls the method very reliable in the Netherlands, citing those two papers (Brunt et al., 2017). Over the years, among 33,006 tablets sold as ecstasy that people handed in at Dutch test offices in 1993–2008 and that were analysed in the laboratory (tablets identified by look and not sent to the laboratory are not among them), the share holding only MDMA as the active drug ranged from 44 in 100 in 1997 to 86 in 100 on average in 2000–2004; the yearly median of MDMA in a tablet ranged from 60 mg (1998) to 84 mg (1994), and single tablets held from traces (under 1 mg) to 225 mg (Vogels et al., 2009). These are amounts measured in tablets, not amounts to take. By the system's authors' statements, which give no counts, only 30 in 100 tablets handed in during October 1997 held MDMA or a similar drug, and only 40 in 100 in March 2009 held MDMA (Brunt & Niesink, 2011). What tablets sold as ecstasy held at seven European drug-checking services in 2008–2013 is in the answer on whether ecstasy is really MDMA. All four papers are by, or led by, the team that runs DIMS, whose database is the reference in the online study. The tablets are those people chose to bring in, which the authors think over-represents tablets whose effects were not what people expected. The online study covers two websites in one country over two years; it gives no count of reports found, excluded or left without a matching tablet, does not say how a value was chosen when several tablets matched or whether the scorers agreed, and defines 'dangerous' differently in its abstract, methods and discussion; its authors caution that people in the Netherlands may be better informed about drug content than elsewhere. The only source these papers cite for how much tablets of the same appearance vary (Cole et al., 2002) was not read. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Online reports about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market posted on Pillreports.net (218) and Partyflock.nl (253) between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2015 (471 reports; who posted them is unknown); tablets sold as ecstasy that people handed in at Dutch DIMS test offices, 33,006 of them analysed in the laboratory in 1993–2008, with the system's statements to July 2010; and the identification of tablets by look at Dutch test offices and, as described, at European drug-checking services in 2008–2013
lines.exposure: A tablet's logo and other visible features (shape, colour, size, weight): as described, with or without a picture, in online reports; and as used, with a Marquis colour test, by Dutch test-office staff to recognise tablets on a weekly updated list of tablets recently analysed in the laboratory
lines.comparator: Laboratory analysis of tablets handed in to DIMS (gas chromatography–mass spectrometry and other methods): for online reports, tablets fitting the report's description handed in within 12 weeks before or after it, not the tablet the report described; no study compared tablets that share a logo with each other, and the validation data for recognition by look are unpublished
lines.outcome: Share of online reports whose stated MDMA amount was more than 10 mg above or below (or more than 40 mg below) the laboratory value for matching tablets, that left out substances found in them, or that the authors scored as 'dangerous'; share whose description fitted more than one distinct tablet; report features (picture, range of amounts) associated with 'dangerous' reports; look-alike tablets holding other drugs (no counts); share of tablets identified by look and its stated reliability; content of laboratory-analysed tablets sold as ecstasy by year (share with only MDMA; MDMA per tablet)
lines.magnitude: Vrolijk et al. (2017): 471 online reports (Pillreports.net 218, Partyflock.nl 253), 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2015, each compared with DIMS laboratory records (GC–MS) of tablets fitting its description handed in within 12 weeks before or after it; percentages with 95% bootstrap CIs (1,000 samples; Table 1): MDMA stated more than 10 mg too high 39.7% (35.2–44.4; Pillreports 47.7, Partyflock 32.8; χ² 10.86, P = 0.001); more than 10 mg too low 17.6% (14.0–21.2); more than 40 mg too low 10.2% (7.6–13.0); unreported substance 15.5% (12.3–18.9); unreported substance scored dangerous 7.0% (4.7–9.3); 'dangerous' overall 15.3% (11.9–18.5); mean difference 10.6 mg too high (6.7–14.4); within 10 mg or no amount given: not reported, at most 42.7% (editors' calculation, 100 − 39.7 − 17.6). Multiple database hits 10.8% (8.1–13.6); picture included 46.9% (42.3–51.2); picture with multiple hits Exp(b) 0.298 (0.111–0.799), P = 0.016; multiple hits with more than 40 mg too low 4.880 (1.608–14.81), P = 0.005, and with an unreported substance 2.556 (1.056–6.186), P = 0.037; multiple hits with 'dangerous' χ² 34.26, P < 0.001; picture with 'dangerous' 1.044 (0.490–2.225), P = 0.912. Range given in 66.2% (61.8–70.1); range with 'dangerous' Exp(b) 0.511 (0.307–0.850), P = 0.010; Pearson χ² 6.890 (printed P 0.007). Editors' reconstruction from Table 1 and the site totals (range 148 + 164 = 312, none 159; 'dangerous' 32 + 40 = 72; data/verification/pdf-2026-11-26/754_calculations.py): 'dangerous' in 34 of 159 reports without a range (21.4%) and 38 of 312 with one (12.2%), the only split that gives Pearson χ² 6.890; ratio of proportions about 1.76, odds ratio about 1.96 (= 1/0.511), the paper's 'approximately twice as likely'. Vogels et al. (2009): 33,006 laboratory-analysed tablets sold as ecstasy, 1993–2008; only MDMA as active substance 44% (1997) to 86% on average (2000–2004); median MDMA per tablet 73 mg over the period, yearly 60 mg (1998) to 84 mg (1994); single tablets from under 1 mg (traces) to 225 mg (tablet contents, not doses). Identification by look and a Marquis test against a weekly list: on average 30% of tablets; reliability stated as 99% from internal checks, without data (Vogels et al., 2009; Brunt & Niesink, 2011); called very reliable in the Netherlands, citing those two papers (Brunt et al., 2017). Brunt & Niesink (2011): tablets with MDMA or an MDMA-like substance 30% in October 1997 and tablets with MDMA 40% in March 2009 (monthly lows, no denominators); 2C-B in tablets resembling ecstasy, with similar logos, shapes and colours, in the second half of the 2000s, and amphetamine in tablets with logos similar to ecstasy (no counts). No paper reports how content varied among tablets sharing a logo.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive (shares of online reports and of tablets): starts low and is never upgraded; risk of bias −1 and indirectness −1 (see the domain notes); very low. It is not rated as a test-accuracy study (METHODS 6.3): an online report is not a test, and the laboratory reference was not applied to the tablet each report described. Status single study: the accuracy of online reports rests on one study; Vogels et al. (2009), Brunt and Niesink (2011) and Brunt et al. (2017) are successive publications of the same Dutch monitoring system and team (Brunt is an author of all four papers, Niesink of three), describe other things (what tablets held; how tablets are identified by look) and do not replicate it. The answer to the question, that nobody has shown that a logo or look tells what a tablet holds, rests on the absence of a study, not on a finding against it: the Dutch system's recognition by measurements, logo and a colour test against recently analysed tablets is not shown to be unreliable either, but its reliability is unpublished (editors' reading). The 21 against 12 in 100 is an editors' reconstruction that reproduces the paper's chi-square exactly; the paper's 'approximately twice as likely' is the odds ratio. Rule 0 ('I barely felt it'): the statement names overstated reports as one possible reason someone felt little from a pill and says these studies did not look at other reasons or at what happens when people then take more; it gives no advice, and the amounts are tablet contents, not doses.

lines.q: Can a pill's logo or look tell you what's in it?
lines.short: Nobody has shown it can. In a Dutch check, about 40 in 100 online pill reports claimed over 10 mg more MDMA than lab tests found in matching pills.
lines.but: Nobody has measured how much pills with the same logo differ. And the online check is one Dutch study of two websites.
how: Staff of the Dutch testing service compared 471 online reports about ecstasy pills from 2014–15 with lab results for pills matching each description. About 40 in 100 said over 10 mg too much MDMA, 18 in 100 over 10 mg too little, and 16 in 100 missed another drug.

The authors called 15 in 100 reports dangerous: far too little MDMA, or a drug left out. Saying too much wasn't counted. A photo helped find the right pill but didn't make reports less often dangerous. Reports giving a range were dangerous less often: 12 against 21 in 100.

The same testers say pills that looked like ecstasy, with similar logos, have held 2C-B or amphetamine. They identify some pills by exact size, weight, logo and a colour test, against pills tested in recent weeks. They call it 99% reliable but have published no data.

In lab tests of Dutch pills sold as ecstasy from 1993 to 2008, only MDMA was found in 44 in 100 in 1997 and about 86 in 100 in 2000–04. Single pills held from a trace to 225 mg. These are lab amounts, not amounts to take.

lines.statement: In laboratory studies in which adults first sampled a benzodiazepine and a dummy pill (placebo) and then chose which to take, a history of problem drug use (the papers' 'drug abuse') is associated with choosing the benzodiazepine: volunteers without such a history mostly chose the placebo, and diazepam calmed and sedated them without raising euphoria scores, while people with such a history almost always chose the benzodiazepine, though they were tested in separate studies by another laboratory, mostly at much higher doses, so their history and the dose cannot be told apart. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team (each kind of person was studied mainly by one laboratory, and no study read compared people with and without such a history at the same doses). In the one primary study read (de Wit et al., 1986, University of Chicago), 36 paid volunteers aged 21 to 35, recruited through advertisements and posters on a university campus and by word of mouth, told that the study offered money and not treatment, and excluded if they had a history of problem drug use, major depression, bipolar disorder or schizophrenia (12 without anxiety, 11 with anxious mood and 13 with generalized anxiety disorder; 6 others did not finish, one of them because of diazepam's sedative effects), each took part in three experiments in counterbalanced order: diazepam (Valium) 5 mg, diazepam 10 mg and d,l-amphetamine 5 mg, each against a placebo capsule of another colour (study conditions). They swallowed one capsule between 9 and 10 in the morning and then went about their day; after four sampling sessions they chose which colour to take on five more occasions. Most chose the placebo: at 5 mg, 21 of the 36 chose diazepam at most once and 8 chose it four or five times; at 10 mg, 27 chose it at most once and 5 four or five times (the numbers fell across the choice categories: z = −2.2, P < .03, and z = −3.0, P < .004), whereas 20 of the 36 chose amphetamine four or five times (z = 2.3, P < .02). The anxious groups chose no differently from the others, but with 11 to 13 people a group only large differences could have been seen (editors' note). Among people who liked one capsule better during the sampling sessions, more liked the placebo: 17 against 8 at 5 mg and 21 against 9 at 10 mg (editors' sums from Table 5). Diazepam lowered ratings of anxiety, vigour and arousal and raised ratings of confusion and sedation, 10 mg also raised fatigue, and on 10 mg days depression and dysphoria scores were higher and friendliness, elation and positive mood scores lower than on placebo days; the euphoria scale did not change significantly at either dose, while amphetamine raised it. Most people recognised 10 mg diazepam as a tranquilizer (30 of 36). The volunteers were not new to drugs (29 of the 36 had used marijuana, 19 stimulants and 6 tranquilizers outside medical care, and 9 drank more than 7 drinks a week; editors' sums from Table 2), but choice was not analysed by drinking or drug history. The authors' conclusion that highly anxious people are not at greater risk of dependence goes beyond what was tested, single morning doses on separate days; they add that people in acute distress, people less bothered by sedation, people expecting a particular effect and people with much earlier sedative or alcohol use might respond differently. A narrative review of laboratory studies published up to 1997, by two authors at Johns Hopkins University (Griffiths & Weerts, 1997; no stated search; its figures are second-hand here, as the primary papers were not read), calls a person's history the most important single factor in whether a benzodiazepine is chosen. In 13 studies of people with 'histories of drug abuse' (2 to 16 people each, men in all but one, 11 of the 13 co-authored by the review's first author; editors' counts from Table 2 and the reference list), the benzodiazepine was almost always chosen, or taken more than its comparison: for example, 16 men chose diazepam over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% of occasions; but four of the 13 studies had no placebo comparison (editors' count), triazolam was taken more than placebo by 4 of 6 men in one study, and in another all 8 men chose triazolam before a relaxation task and none before a vigilance task. In 17 studies of people without such histories (12 with de Wit or Johanson of the Chicago group among the authors; editors' count), healthy volunteers who were light drinkers without anxiety or insomnia consistently did not choose a benzodiazepine over placebo (for example diazepam on 25% to 38% of choice sessions in four studies, lorazepam on 16% and flurazepam on 20%), in several studies choosing it significantly less often than placebo, while amphetamine was chosen under similar conditions. Most of the studies in people with histories of problem drug use gave much higher doses (for example diazepam 40 to 400 mg in three of them, against diazepam in single doses of 2 to 20 mg or in 4 mg capsules taken one at a time in the studies of other volunteers; study conditions), and the review itself reports that choice depended on dose, yet it does not discuss dose as an explanation of the difference between the two kinds of people (editors' reading). What the review counts as a drug being chosen for its effects (reinforcement) covers any reason, whether to feel good, to ease anxiety or to avoid withdrawal, so choosing a benzodiazepine does not by itself show that people felt high. Moderate social drinkers (about 12 drinks a week) chose diazepam over placebo in three studies, on 100%, 73% and 64% of choices, while light drinkers (about 4 a week), tested under the same procedure in two of them, did not significantly prefer it (66%, a non-significant tendency, and 40%; the difference from moderate drinkers significant in the second); the moderate drinkers more often used marijuana weekly, and the review says that people with a history of moderate drinking or of alcoholism showed greater positive mood effects from benzodiazepines (no figures given), while calling what the drinkers' preference means for real-life risk unclear. In anxious people the results were mixed and lined up with how the drug was offered: two studies with a single morning dose found no preference (de Wit et al., 1986, and 14 people seeking treatment, who chose diazepam on 37% of sessions), while three that let people decide when and how many capsules to take found one (65% of evening sessions in 22 anxious volunteers against 45% in 23 volunteers without anxiety, P = 0.06; 3 of 4 women with generalized anxiety disorder, and 11 of 14 people with generalized anxiety or panic disorder, taking capsules as needed over 4 weeks, mostly at low, stable rates). People with insomnia chose triazolam on 86% of nights when they had to pick it or a placebo at bedtime, but took placebo capsules as often as triazolam when either was simply on offer. The review flags its comparisons across studies as not tested prospectively. As cited by the review, about half of US high-school students who reported non-medical use of tranquilizers (mostly benzodiazepines) said they usually got high from them (a survey report covering 1975 to 1992, with no single year given). In a US national survey of 2015 and 2016, getting high was the main reason given by 11.6% of adults who reported misusing benzodiazepines, behind relaxing and sleep (see the answer on why people misuse benzodiazepines). The laboratory studies date from 1976 to 1997, are small, used capsules prepared by the researchers, and none that the review describes followed whether choosing a benzodiazepine in the laboratory predicts later use outside it.
lines.population: Adults in laboratory choice studies: in the primary study read, 36 paid volunteers aged 21 to 35 at the University of Chicago without a history of problem drug use (12 without anxiety, 11 with anxious mood and 13 with DSM-III generalized anxiety disorder; 22 women); as summarized second-hand by a narrative review of studies published up to 1997, people with histories of problem drug use (13 studies of 2 to 16 people, men in all but one) and people without (17 studies: healthy volunteers, light and moderate social drinkers, people with or without an alcoholic first-degree relative, anxious people, people with insomnia); for context, US adults reporting benzodiazepine misuse in a 2015–2016 national survey
lines.exposure: A benzodiazepine given by the researchers by mouth, mostly double-blind, in capsules of a colour that people learned during sampling sessions (study conditions: in the primary study single morning doses of 5 or 10 mg diazepam on separate days; in the review's studies diazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam, oxazepam, triazolam or flurazepam, mostly at much higher doses in people with histories of problem drug use, for example diazepam 40 to 400 mg in three studies, and diazepam in single doses of 2 to 20 mg or in 4 mg capsules taken one at a time in others)
lines.comparator: Placebo capsules in the same people (a choice between the two colours, or self-administration of each); kinds of people compared across separate studies (problem drug use or not) and within some studies (anxious or not; moderate or light drinkers); d,l-amphetamine 5 mg as a comparison drug in the primary study
lines.outcome: How often the benzodiazepine was chosen or taken rather than placebo; liking ratings; identification of the capsule; mood questionnaires (Profile of Mood States; the ARCI questionnaire with euphoria, sedation and dysphoria scales); for context, the main reason for misuse people gave in a national survey
lines.magnitude: de Wit et al. (1986), 36 people (controls 12, anxious mood 11, generalized anxiety disorder 13), numbers choosing the drug on 0–1, 2–3 and 4–5 of 5 choice sessions: diazepam 5 mg 21, 7, 8 (trend z = −2.2, P < .03); diazepam 10 mg 27, 4, 5 (controls 9, 1, 2; anxious mood 10, 1, 0; generalized anxiety 8, 2, 3; z = −3.0, P < .004); d,l-amphetamine 5 mg 6, 10, 20 (z = 2.3, P < .02); no group differences. Editors' shares: diazepam at most once 58 in 100 (5 mg) and 75 in 100 (10 mg), four or five times 22 and 14 in 100; amphetamine four or five times 56 in 100. Mean amphetamine choices 4.0, 3.1 and 2.9 of 5 (controls, anxious mood, generalized anxiety), about 67% overall (editors' calculation from the printed means; the review's Table 3 estimates 73%). Liking over the sampling sessions (Table 5; equal ratings left out): placebo liked more by 17 and diazepam by 8 at 5 mg (11 equal); by 21 and 9 at 10 mg (5 equal; 35 of the 36 accounted for); choice by liking z = 2.51 (P < .02) at 5 mg; at 10 mg placebo chosen more whichever capsule was liked more, z = 2.63 (P < .01). Identification: 10 mg diazepam called a tranquilizer by 30 of 36, 5 mg by 18 of 32. Mood (Table 6): both doses lowered Anxiety, Vigor, Arousal and the stimulant-like BG scale and raised Confusion and the sedation (PCAG) scale (drug by hour, P = .001 to .04); 10 mg raised Fatigue (P = .001), Depression (P = .03) and the dysphoria (LSD) scale (P = .01) and lowered Friendliness (P = .004), Elation (P = .003) and Positive Mood (P = .003); no significant diazepam effect on the euphoria (MBG) scale; amphetamine on MBG drug by hour P = .001. Background (Table 2; editors' sums): marijuana ever 29, stimulants ever 19, tranquilizers outside medical care ever 6, more than 7 drinks a week 9, of 36. Griffiths & Weerts (1997), as tabulated (second-hand): people with histories of problem drug use, 13 studies, 2 to 16 people each; diazepam chosen over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% (16 men); lorazepam chosen over buspirone by 7 of 8; triazolam a reinforcer in 4 of 6, and chosen before relaxation by 8 of 8 and before a vigilance task by 0 of 8; 4 of 13 studies without a placebo comparison (editors' count). People without such histories, 17 studies: diazepam 28% and 27% of choice sessions (5 and 10 mg; 10 people), 25%, 32% and 38% (three groups), 28% (estimated, de Wit et al., 1986), 33% (43 people); lorazepam 2 mg 16% and flurazepam 30 mg 20% (12 people each); 5 mg d-amphetamine 76%. Moderate against light social drinkers (about 12 against 4 drinks a week): 100% against 66% (12 and 18 people), 73% against 40% (14 and 13; difference significant); moderate drinkers 64% diazepam (30 people) against 27% buspirone (25 others). Anxious people: 37% (14 seeking treatment, single morning dose); 65% against 45% (22 and 23 people; P = 0.06); 3 of 4; 11 of 14. Insomnia: triazolam on 86% of nights under forced choice (three groups of 8); capsules on 77% (triazolam) and 80% (placebo) of nights when only one was available. As cited: about half of US high-school students reporting non-medical tranquilizer use usually got high. Maust et al. (2019): main reason for benzodiazepine misuse to get high 11.6% (13.9% at ages 18–49, 3.0% at 50 or older), against relaxing 47.1% and sleep 26.6%.
lines.reasoning: Rated as observational because the claim is about who chooses benzodiazepines, a comparison between kinds of people made mostly across separate studies (METHODS 6.3; brief for this round), although each study's own comparison of the drug with a placebo is within-person and mostly double-blind. Low start; risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 give very low (the scale stops there). The within-person finding of de Wit et al. (1986) alone, that 36 volunteers without problem drug use, anxious or not, mostly chose a placebo over single morning doses of diazepam, which calmed and sedated them without raising euphoria scores, rests on a counterbalanced, placebo-controlled comparison and a behavioural outcome and would be moderate on its own (high start; imprecision −1: 36 people, no intervals); the same laboratory found the same in other volunteers, as the review summarizes, which is replication by the same team. The contrast with people with problem drug use rests on the review's comparison of separate studies by another laboratory, mostly at much higher doses, and cannot separate history from dose; the statement says so and does not give it as the review's own caution, which it is not. Status replicated by the same team: volunteers without problem drug use were studied mainly by the Chicago group (de Wit, Johanson, Uhlenhuth) and people with problem drug use mainly by the review's first author's group, and no study read compared the two at the same doses. Choosing a drug over a placebo is not the same as feeling high: the review's definition of reinforcement covers any motive, and only de Wit et al. measured euphoria directly. The school-survey figure is second-hand and the national survey figure qualifies the claim without being part of the rating. The review's findings on how fast the drug acts and its comparisons of benzodiazepines by appeal are left out by design. Doses are given only as study conditions; nothing here is advice on amounts or use.

lines.q: Do benzos get you high, and who actually likes them?
lines.short: Depends who you are. In one lab study, 27 of 36 people without drug problems mostly chose a dummy pill over Valium. People with past drug problems almost always chose benzos.
lines.but: But those people were tested in other labs' studies, mostly with much bigger doses. So we can't tell if their past made the difference.
how: In a 1980s study, 36 young volunteers with no history of drug problems (most had tried cannabis) tried Valium and a dummy pill, then chose between them five times. Most picked the dummy pill, anxious or not.
Valium calmed them and made them sleepy and a bit muddled. It didn't raise their scores for euphoria. At the higher dose they felt more tired and less cheerful than on the dummy pill.

A review of older lab studies found that people with a history of drug problems almost always chose benzos. Moderate drinkers chose Valium more than light drinkers did. Anxious people chose benzos when they could take them as needed.

Outside the lab, some people say they get high. A review cites an older US school survey in which about half of teens who took calming pills without a prescription said they usually got high. In a newer adult survey, 12 in 100 who misused benzos said getting high was their main reason.

lines.statement: In people admitted to hospital after a tramadol overdose, seizures were common, consciousness was often reduced and breathing was depressed enough to lower blood oxygen in some, while serotonin toxicity was not seen in the one series that looked for it and few people died in hospital; how often each happened differed widely between settings, many people had taken other medicines too, and no study read measured the risk for a person who takes tramadol. At one Australian toxicology unit (Ryan & Isbister, 2015), 71 admissions (70 people, November 2000 to June 2013) followed more than 400 mg, which the authors give as the maximum daily dose (median reported amount 1,000 mg; amounts and drugs as reported by the patients and others, not confirmed by laboratory tests); 51 had also taken other medicines, among them benzodiazepines (16), SSRI (13) and SNRI (10) antidepressants and tricyclic antidepressants (3). Seizures occurred in 8 of the 71 (11 in 100; exact 95% CI 5 to 21, editors' calculation): in 2 of the 20 who took tramadol alone and 6 of the 51 who took other medicines too, close to the 8 and 14 in 100 of two earlier series of tramadol exposures the authors cite. The first seizure came 1.5 to 22.7 hours after the overdose (median 8.5): 6.5 to 22.7 hours after slow-release tablets against 1.5 to 11 hours after immediate-release ones (8 people). People who had seizures had reported larger amounts (median 2,100 against 1,000 mg; p = 0.018 in the text and 0.021 in the figure legend), and the two seizures after the smallest amounts came with a predisposing reason (benzodiazepine withdrawal; an earlier seizure); but with 8 seizures and self-reported amounts this shows no safe amount, 3 of the 16 admissions left out because the amount was unknown also had seizures, and the authors cite a Tehran study in which seizures were unrelated to the amount, most after 500 to 1,000 mg. Consciousness was reduced (Glasgow Coma Scale below 15) in 29 of 71 (41 in 100) and deeply reduced (below 9, coma) in 5: three after tricyclic antidepressants and two with depressed breathing that responded to naloxone. Respiratory depression with oxygen saturation below 94% occurred in 13 of 71 (18 in 100; 10 to 29, editors' calculation), within 2 hours of the overdose in 7 of the 9 with a known time (5 and 8 hours in the other 2), in people who had reported larger amounts (median 2,500 against 1,000 mg; p = 0.003); 5 of the 13 had also taken a tricyclic antidepressant or promethazine or had pneumonia, and coma and respiratory depression are not reported separately for the 20 who took tramadol alone, although the authors say respiratory depression occurred with tramadol alone. A fast heart rate (no threshold stated) occurred in 27 (38 in 100), systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg in 32 (45 in 100), and vomiting or nausea in 36 (51 in 100). Naloxone, given in hospital to 9 people, improved oxygen levels or consciousness in 6, partly in 2 and not in 1, and no seizure was reported after it. Eight people, all of whom had taken other medicines, went to intensive care (5 for the other medicines' effects, 3 for breathing), and nobody died. No admission met the Hunter criteria for serotonin toxicity, including people who had also taken SSRIs or SNRIs; one person who had also taken an escitalopram overdose had one of its signs (eye clonus) without meeting the criteria. None in 71 rules out only frequencies above about 5 in 100 in such overdoses (exact 95% upper limit 5.1 in 100, editors' calculation) and says nothing about tramadol at ordinary amounts or taken with antidepressants over time: the reports of serotonin toxicity the authors cite mostly involve tramadol taken with serotonergic antidepressants, and their conclusion about therapeutic doses goes beyond their data (reactions reported with MAOI antidepressants are covered in the answer on opioid painkillers taken with MAOIs). In Iran, a systematic review pooled hospital and poison-centre series of people admitted with tramadol poisoning, mostly young men, with a suicide attempt the commonest reason in most series that reported one and tramadol taken alone by 43 to 100 in 100 where this was reported (Rostam-Abadi et al., 2020): seizures were recorded in a pooled 34.6 in 100 (95% CI 29.6 to 39.8; 23 series, 5,972 admissions by the editors' sum; I² 94%), from about 12 to 69 in 100 in single series, with a prediction interval, the range in which a new series would be expected to fall, of 12.5 to 60.9 (read from the forest plot). Deaths in hospital were a pooled 0.7 in 100, or 7 in 1,000 (95% CI 0.0 to 1.9 in 100; 18 series, 4,761 admissions by the editors' sum; I² 92%; prediction interval 0 to 10.0 in 100): six series had none, and one series of 1,023 people in Kermanshah had 10 in 100, against 0.9 in 100 in a series of 546 from the same city and overlapping years. Breathing was reported unevenly: apnoea was among the three commonest other features listed for four series (3.6 to 6.2 in 100 in three, and 15.0 in 100 in a series of 20 children) and slowed breathing (18 in 100) for one, and changes in consciousness were among the commonest features. In four Iranian emergency departments and hospitals, tramadol poisoning was recorded in 22 in 100 first seizures (383 people), 37 in 100 of all seizures (141) and 40 and 55 in 100 of drug-induced seizures (143 and 137). The Iranian seizure figures are about three times the Australian one: the Australian authors suggest that some Tehran series drew patients selected for seizures, and the review's authors suggest that many people in Iran convert tramadol fast through a liver enzyme (CYP2D6), which no included study measured. The review found no study of poisoning or death among people who use tramadol; it was not preregistered and its authors call it exploratory; whether tramadol was confirmed by laboratory tests was not extracted; several series come from the same cities and periods and may count the same patients; and its pooled figures mix tramadol-only and mixed poisonings. Seizures at ordinary amounts were not measured in these papers and appear only in reports: in Iran's national reports of reactions blamed on tramadol (249 people, 2006–2010, 22.8 in 100 of the reports classed as prescribed use), seizure was the reaction most often reported (29.3 in 100 in the text, 29.5 in its table), and one case report describes a seizure after 200 mg by mouth with no other drug. Some people feel little from an amount of tramadol, and some then take more: the papers say, citing other work, that tramadol works largely through a breakdown product (O-desmethyltramadol) made by CYP2D6, whose activity differs between people with their genes and other medicines, and in the Australian series people who had seizures or low oxygen had reported larger amounts. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: People admitted to hospital after a tramadol overdose: 71 admissions (70 people) after more than 400 mg at one Australian toxicology unit, November 2000 to June 2013; Iranian hospital and poison-centre series of people admitted with tramadol poisoning, mostly 2004–2017 and mostly young men (23 series, 5,972 admissions, for seizures; 18 series, 4,761, for deaths); and, for seizures outside an overdose, Iranian adverse-reaction reports and one case report
lines.exposure: Tramadol overdose (in the Australian series more than 400 mg, median reported 1,000 mg, with other medicines in 51 of 71); in the Iranian series tramadol poisoning, taken alone by 43 to 100 in 100 where reported
lines.comparator: None outside the series (no comparison with other overdoses or with people taking tramadol without an overdose); within the Australian series, admissions after tramadol alone against those with other medicines, and reported amounts with and without seizures or respiratory depression

Glasgow Coma Scale below 15: 29/71 (41%; 29.3–53.2); below 9: 5/71 (7%; 2.3–15.7), 3 after tricyclics. Respiratory depression (oxygen saturation below 94%): 13/71 (18%; 10.1–29.3, editors' calculation), onset 2 h or less in 7 of 9 with a known time; reported amount 2,500 (1,600–3,000) against 1,000 mg (750–1,475), p = 0.003; 5 of 13 with a tricyclic, promethazine or pneumonia (Figure 4). Tachycardia 27 (38%); systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg 32 (45%); vomiting or nausea 36 (51%). Naloxone given to 9: improved 6, partly 2, not 1. Intensive care 8 (all after co-ingestion: 5 co-ingestant toxicity, 3 respiratory depression); deaths 0/71 (0–5.1%). Hunter serotonin toxicity 0/71 (exact 95% upper limit 5.1%, editors' calculation; one-sided 95% upper limit 4.1%). Rostam-Abadi et al. (2020), Iranian admissions with tramadol poisoning: seizures pooled 34.6% (95% CI 29.6–39.8), I² 94.0%, 23 series (5,972 admissions, editors' sum of the sample sizes in Figure 5), single series 11.7–69.3% (12.0–69.3% in the text), prediction interval 12.5–60.9% (Figure 5); deaths pooled 0.7% (0.0–1.9), I² 91.7%, 18 series (4,761 admissions, editors' sum from Figure 6), prediction interval 0–10.0%, six series with none, the highest 10.0% (Kermanshah, 1,023) against 0.9% (Kermanshah, 546, overlapping years); by the editors' approximation from the rounded proportions in Figure 6, about 129 deaths in all, about 102 of them in the 10.0% series. Table 5: apnoea 4.7%, 3.6%, 6.2% and 15.0% (20 children) in the four series that list it; bradypnoea 18.0% in one; tramadol alone in 43.0–100% of cases where reported. Table 4: tramadol poisoning in 21.9% of 383 first seizures, 36.8% of 141 seizures, 39.5% of 143 and 54.7% of 137 drug-induced seizures. National adverse-reaction reports, 2006–10: 249 people, seizure the most reported reaction (29.3% in the text, 29.5% in Table 5). One case report: seizure after 200 mg by mouth, no other drug (Table 6).
lines.reasoning: Descriptive (frequencies among hospital admissions after a tramadol overdose): starts low; down one level for risk of bias and one for inconsistency; very low; never upgraded (descriptive claims are not). Status replicated: seizures in a substantial share of admissions were found independently in the Australian series and in the Iranian series (counted once, as one review), in the same direction but at very different frequencies. The figures for consciousness, respiratory depression, naloxone and the absence of serotonin toxicity rest on the Australian series alone (single study); the Iranian breathing data are listed for only five series, as one of each series' three commonest other features. The pooled Iranian death figure (0.7 in 100) gives the series similar weights; most of the deaths in the pooled series come from one series of 1,023 with 10 in 100 (editors' approximation from Figure 6). Seizures at ordinary amounts were not measured in any study read: the adverse-reaction reports and the case report show only that such seizures were reported. The sentence on feeling little rests on background statements both papers cite, not on their own measurements.

lines.q: Can tramadol cause seizures, and what happens in an overdose?
lines.short: In overdoses, seizures are common. 11 in 100 people treated at one Australian unit had them, and about 35 in 100 in Iran. Some had trouble breathing too.
lines.but: These were overdoses, often with other pills too. No one checked the risk at normal doses.
how: At one Australian hospital unit, 8 of 71 people treated for a tramadol overdose had seizures. That was 2 of the 20 who took only tramadol, and 6 of the 51 who took other pills too. Some came almost a day later.

18 in 100 had breathing trouble with low oxygen, and 5 went into a coma (3 of them had also taken an older type of antidepressant). Those who said they took more had more seizures and breathing trouble. Nobody died.
No one met the criteria for serotonin syndrome. With 71 people, that only rules out rates above about 5 in 100. Earlier reported cases mostly involved tramadol taken with antidepressants.
In 23 Iranian hospital studies, about 35 in 100 had seizures, but single studies ranged from 12 to 69 in 100. About 7 in 1,000 died in hospital; one study had 100 in 1,000.

lines.statement: Some medicines, their breakdown products and a few foods and other products have been reported to make particular urine drug screens read positive when the drug screened for was absent, as described second-hand in two narrative reviews: a review by laboratory-medicine authors of reports published from 2000 on, with a stated search that found 173 articles, 62 of them with data on false positives (Saitman et al., 2014), and a clinical review for clinicians (Moeller et al., 2017). Screens are immunoassays: they use antibodies, which can also bind other substances, including ones whose structure looks unlike the target, and breakdown products. Each report concerns particular tests, and the same medicine often left other tests unaffected; most reports are single case reports, reviews of patients' charts, or experiments adding a medicine to drug-free urine, and some concern tests that have since changed. Examples with counts: in a blinded study, one point-of-care benzodiazepine test was positive in 46 of 50 people taking the HIV medicine efavirenz and negative in 47 of 50 not taking it, while two other point-of-care tests and LC-MS/MS were negative on all the positives; efavirenz also gave false-positive cannabis screens through a breakdown product on three immunoassays, and in another study one brand of test strips was positive in 28 of 30 people taking it while another device and two laboratory assays were negative; and one laboratory amphetamine assay was negative in 6 healthy men before two doses of the antibiotic ofloxacin and positive in all 6 after. By screen, the reviews name, among others: for amphetamine screens, which the clinical review calls the screens most often linked to false positives, pseudoephedrine and ephedrine, bupropion, labetalol, ranitidine, metformin, the supplement DMAA and trazodone (through its breakdown product, on one ecstasy screen and one amphetamine screen but not another), in a table of 33 entries (among them phentermine, methylphenidate and atomoxetine) that mixes false positives with true ones such as prescribed dextroamphetamine and names no tests or frequencies; for benzodiazepine screens, sertraline, efavirenz and oxaprozin; for cannabis screens, efavirenz, NSAID painkillers (2 false positives in 510 samples in one study, called rare), proton pump inhibitors (one case report and a package insert) and, in newborns' urine, several baby wash products at a 20 ng/mL cutoff; for opiate screens, quinolone antibiotics, rifampicin, naloxone added to urine at high concentrations, and poppy seeds (the US federal workplace cutoff for morphine was raised from 300 to 2,000 ng/mL in 1998 to limit positives from poppy seeds and prescribed opiates); for PCP screens, venlafaxine, dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine and tramadol (in case reports, after overdose), the laboratory review adding that a positive PCP screen is rarely a true positive because PCP use is rare and the tests are not specific; for methadone screens, quetiapine, verapamil, diphenhydramine and doxylamine; and for buprenorphine screens, morphine and other opioids added to urine, so that heroin use could make a buprenorphine screen read positive. Only a few frequencies are printed, and none is the chance that a person taking a medicine will screen positive: in one chart review, 41% of amphetamine screens that GC-MS did not confirm (53 patients; the total is not printed) came from people taking bupropion, with no experiment showing that bupropion caused it; in another, 26.5% of benzodiazepine screens that confirmation did not support (26 samples) were linked to sertraline, again without such an experiment (the clinical review gives 27% to 32% from two chart reviews without saying of what); and in a US Department of Defense analysis the supplement DMAA was found in 92.3% of false-positive amphetamine samples. Some medicines give true positives because they are, or turn into, the substance tested for: prescribed amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine on amphetamine screens; dronabinol, a prescribed form of THC, on cannabis screens, which confirmation cannot tell from cannabis; and codeine, which the body turns partly into morphine. Cocaine screens cross-react little: the clinical review finds no evidence for the claim that amoxicillin makes them positive (four immunoassays tested showed none) and says that numbing medicines such as lidocaine, benzocaine, procaine and tetracaine do not, whereas cocaine used as a medical anaesthetic gives true positives and coca leaf tea can make cocaine screens positive. Alcohol tests for ethyl glucuronide can turn positive after hand sanitizer or mouthwash. Both reviews say a screen is presumptive and should be confirmed by a different method, such as GC-MS or LC-MS/MS, which identifies the substance: the clinical review advises always confirming before legal, employment or other decisions with serious consequences, and the laboratory review notes that such testing is limited or absent in many hospital laboratories and takes days, so decisions are often made on unconfirmed screens. The reviews disagree on one test: the clinical review says efavirenz affects the Drug Screen Multi 5 benzodiazepine test, citing the blinded study and another, while the laboratory review reports that test as negative on the efavirenz positives in the blinded study. The laboratory review also says, without data, that in most cases the cause of a false-positive screen is unknown. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: People whose urine was screened for drugs while taking medicines, or after eating or using products, that might react with the screen, as described second-hand in two narrative reviews of published case reports, chart reviews and dosing studies, and of laboratory experiments adding medicines to drug-free urine (reports published from 2000 on in one review; literature from 1946 to 2016 in the other)
lines.exposure: Medicines and their breakdown products (among them efavirenz, sertraline, bupropion, labetalol, pseudoephedrine, trazodone, quinolone antibiotics, rifampicin, venlafaxine, tramadol, dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine, quetiapine and NSAIDs), a supplement (DMAA), foods (poppy seeds, coca leaf tea) and products (baby wash, hand sanitizer, mouthwash) in urine tested with named screening immunoassays
lines.comparator: Confirmation by a different method (GC-MS, LC-MS/MS or another chromatographic method) showing the target drug absent; drug-free urine before a medicine was added; urine before dosing; in one blinded study, people not taking the medicine
lines.outcome: False-positive screening results (a positive immunoassay screen without the target drug) on named tests, the concentration at which they occurred where tested, and how often, where printed; true positives from medicines that are, or become, the substance tested for
lines.magnitude: Saitman et al. (2014), as described: efavirenz, Biosite Triage 8 benzodiazepine test, blinded, 46 of 50 taking efavirenz positive and 47 of 50 not taking it negative; Drug Control 008, Drug Screen Multi 5 and LC-MS/MS negative on all presumptive positives; efavirenz, Rapid Response cannabis test strips positive in 28 of 30 people taking it for at least 2 weeks, the other point-of-care device and two automated assays negative; ofloxacin, one amphetamine assay (Abbott TDxFLx), 0 of 6 samples positive before and 6 of 6 after two doses in healthy men, the lowest almost four times the 300 ng/mL cutoff; promethazine and chlorpromazine, 3 and 6 specimens positive on Syva EMIT-MAM and negative by LC-PDA, all 9 negative on Syva EMIT-A and Biosite Triage, 2 positive on Agilent TesTcard 9; bupropion, 41% (53 patients) of Syva EMIT II Plus amphetamine positives not confirmed by GC-MS, total not printed (about 129 if 53 is 41%, editors' arithmetic), no spiking; sertraline, 26.5% (26 samples) of benzodiazepine screens positive on the Abbott Architect and Aeroset and negative on confirmation, January 2007 to December 2008, no spiking (about 98 false positives in all if 26 is 26.5%, editors' arithmetic); niflumic acid, 55 of 55 samples from 5 volunteers positive on Roche KIMS THC and negative on Syva EMIT; ambroxol, unexpected positive LSD screens (CEDIA) in twelve patients; buprenorphine screen (CEDIA, 5 ng/mL) and tramadol, false positives removed by a 20 ng/mL cutoff. Moeller et al. (2017), as described: sertraline and benzodiazepine screens, 27% to 32% in two retrospective studies, denominators not stated; NSAIDs and cannabis screens, 2 false positives in 510 samples (one with ibuprofen, one with naproxen; Saitman et al. list the same study's ibuprofen and naproxen results as case reports); PCP screens, false-positive rates of 24% with dextromethorphan, 22% with tramadol and 15% with diphenhydramine in urines not confirmed by GC-MS, denominators not stated; DMAA in 92.3% of false-positive amphetamine samples confirmed negative by GC-MS (US Department of Defense analysis); amoxicillin, no false-positive cocaine results on 4 immunoassays; federal opiate (morphine) screening cutoff raised from 300 to 2,000 ng/mL in 1998; Table 4, 33 entries for amphetamine screens (editors' count), mixing true and false positives, with no tests, concentrations or frequencies.
lines.reasoning: Reports of false-positive screens are case reports, chart reviews, small dosing studies and laboratory experiments, seen here only through two narrative reviews: they start low (METHODS §6.3: claims seen only through reviews start from the design of the primary studies and are rated down for risk of bias and indirectness); risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 take the claim to very low, the floor. It rests only on narrative reviews, so it stays at draft and says that its figures are second-hand. The rule for test accuracy (METHODS §6.3) was considered and not applied: the claim says which medicines were reported to cause false positives on which tests, not how often a test reads right; the one accuracy-type comparison, efavirenz on one benzodiazepine test in 100 people with LC-MS/MS as the reference, is seen second-hand. Status replicated: separate reports by different teams, described in both reviews, agree that particular medicines can make particular screens read positive when confirmation finds no drug (efavirenz on cannabis screens in two studies, quinolone antibiotics on opiate screens in several); most single medicine-and-test pairs rest on one report, and the two reviews share sources, counted once. Nothing is phrased as advice on avoiding or passing a test; the clinical review's section on tampering with samples was not used.

lines.q: Can medicines cause a false positive on a drug test?
lines.short: Yes, some can, on certain tests. On one benzo test, 46 of 50 people taking the HIV drug efavirenz screened positive, but a lab check found no benzos.
lines.but: Most reports describe one or a few people, or a medicine added to urine in a lab. No one has counted how often it happens to people who take them.
how: Quick screens use antibodies, which can grab molecules that look alike. Reviews name sertraline for benzo tests. They name bupropion and pseudoephedrine for amphetamine tests, and some antibiotics for opiate tests.
Only a few numbers exist. In two chart reviews, 41 in 100 unconfirmed amphetamine screens came from people taking bupropion, and about 27 in 100 false benzo screens were linked to sertraline.

Some medicines give true positives, because they are or become the drug tested. Examples: prescribed amphetamines, prescribed THC, and codeine, which turns into morphine. There is no evidence that amoxicillin trips a cocaine test. Numbing drugs like lidocaine do not.
Both reviews say a screen is only a first step. A different lab method should check it before a big decision, like a job or a court case.

lines.statement: In people with opioid dependence who entered methadone maintenance treatment in high-income countries, periods out of treatment were associated with higher death rates than periods in treatment, with the highest rates in the first four weeks after leaving; three buprenorphine cohorts showed a similar but less certain pattern. A systematic review pooled 19 cohorts published 1974–2016 (18 methadone cohorts, 122,885 people, followed 1965–2010; 3 buprenorphine cohorts, 15,831 people, 1990–2010; 11 in Europe or Israel, 4 in North America, 4 in Australia), counting time in and out of treatment for the same people (Sordo et al., 2017). With methadone, the pooled all-cause death rate was 11.3 per 1,000 person-years in treatment (95% CI 8.4 to 15.2) and 36.1 out of treatment (24.5 to 53.3), an unadjusted difference of 24.9 (13.6 to 36.1) and a ratio of 3.20 (2.65 to 3.86), in 16 cohorts; every cohort had a higher rate out of treatment (cohort rates 5.1 to 39.5 in treatment and 12.4 to 130.2 out). These pooled figures are random-effects averages across very different cohorts (I² 98%): in the three largest, recent register cohorts, which hold 83% of the person-years, the differences were 5.5 to 11.2 and the ratios 1.8 to 2.7, and adding up all deaths and person-years gives 7.1 against 16.4 (editors' calculations from the per-cohort figures). Overdose deaths with methadone (11 cohorts) were 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) in treatment against 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4) out, a difference of 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4) and a ratio of 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96), higher out of treatment in every cohort. By time since starting or leaving methadone (five recent cohorts, after the review left out one cohort of people with HIV who inject; one cohort split at two weeks instead of four), the rate was 11.4 (5.8 to 22.4) in the first four weeks of treatment against 5.8 (5.0 to 6.7) for the rest of treatment, a ratio of 1.97 (0.94 to 4.10) that was not statistically significant; and 32.1 (19.1 to 53.9) in the first four weeks after leaving against 13.5 (11.9 to 15.3) for the rest of the time out of treatment, a difference of 18.6 (2.9 to 34.3) and a ratio of 2.38 (1.51 to 3.74), higher in the first period in each of the five cohorts; the review did not compare the weeks after leaving with time in treatment directly. The rise after leaving was seen in deaths from all causes: in the three methadone cohorts that gave overdose deaths by period, the overdose rate was 4.2 (1.8 to 9.9) in the first four weeks after leaving against 3.4 (2.3 to 5.1) later, from 20 overdose deaths in the first period, and in the two cohorts that gave both counts, 18 of the 79 deaths in the first four weeks after leaving were counted as overdoses (editors' count and calculation); the authors expect overdose deaths to be undercounted and note that deaths from suicide and injury are also more common in that period. With buprenorphine (3 cohorts; 96% of the deaths from Australian studies), the rate was 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) in treatment against 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4) out (difference 5.2, −1.0 to 11.4; ratio 2.20, 1.34 to 3.61), 4.5 both in the first four weeks and in the rest of treatment, and 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) in the first four weeks after leaving against 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9) later (two cohorts; difference 21.2, −5.9 to 48.2). All pooled estimates are unadjusted; in the cohorts that reported ratios adjusted for demographics, severity of drug use, treatment or illness (five methadone and one buprenorphine cohort for all causes), the ratios were unchanged or larger. But people leave and re-enter treatment for reasons that may themselves affect their risk; the review had no data on why people left or on tolerance or drug use after leaving, and its pooled results do not separate people who finished treatment from people who dropped out or were discharged. Only an appendix table does, for three methadone cohorts, without saying what made treatment 'complete' or 'incomplete': in a nationwide Swedish cohort of 166 people followed 1967–87 and a Tel Aviv cohort of 613 people followed 1993–2008, death rates over the whole time out of treatment were 69.1 against 16.5 per 1,000 person-years after incomplete against complete treatment (26 against 6 deaths; ratio 4.19, 1.72 to 10.18; overdose deaths 58.5 against 13.7, from 22 and 5 deaths) and 83.5 against 25.6 (47 against 5 deaths; ratio 3.26, 1.30 to 8.21), while a UK cohort that counted only the first four weeks after leaving, with methadone and buprenorphine together, found no clear difference (ratio 0.95, 0.24 to 3.73); these comparisons are unadjusted, set different people against each other and rest on few deaths, and the review names the table in its methods without reporting or discussing it. People lost to follow-up may be at higher risk; medicines obtained outside treatment were not captured; and people in prison or recently released, in detoxification or never treated were excluded. The authors suggest that loss of tolerance, assuming many people return to use, and the use of several substances may explain the rise after leaving. The discussion's statement that death rates were significantly lower with buprenorphine than with methadone has no test or estimate in the results. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

lines.reasoning: Cohort studies are observational and start low; downgraded one level for risk of bias because the claim is seen only through one review, rated critically low, and the cohorts themselves were not read (METHODS §6.3, claims seen only through reviews): very low. Not downgraded further: the review prints each cohort's data, the direction holds in all 16 methadone cohorts for all causes and all 11 for overdose, and adjustment in six cohorts left the ratios unchanged or larger. The start of methadone treatment (not statistically significant), the buprenorphine figures (three cohorts, mostly one Australian study) and the overdose figures by period (three cohorts) are worded as uncertain and not rated separately. Whether treatment prevents deaths, or stopping causes them, is not claimed. The appendix comparison of complete against incomplete treatment (three cohorts, unadjusted, few deaths, not discussed by the review) is given as a description and not rated separately. Status: replicated (16 methadone cohorts from different countries and teams, same direction); one review read, with its appendices.

lines.q: Is it dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine (Suboxone)?
lines.short: Deaths were more common off treatment, most of all in the first 4 weeks after leaving. In 16 methadone studies, about 36 in 1,000 died a year off treatment, against 11 on it.
lines.but: The main figures lump together everyone who left, for any reason. People who leave differ in other ways. So the studies can't show that stopping itself caused the deaths.
how: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. Every group had more deaths out of treatment, though in the biggest recent groups the gap was smaller: about 6 or 7 a year, against 12 to 18.

5 recent studies, with lower death rates overall, split deaths by time: about 32 a year per 1,000 people in the first 4 weeks off methadone, against about 14 later on. The first 4 weeks on it looked riskier too, but that could be chance.

With buprenorphine, almost all the deaths came from Australian studies. Deaths were also higher in the first 4 weeks off, about 32 against 11 a year per 1,000, but that's from just two studies. Counting overdoses alone, 3 methadone studies found no clear rise in those weeks, but only 20 happened then.

Did finishing treatment matter? Only 3 studies looked, and the review doesn't say what finishing meant. In two small ones, deaths after leaving ran 3 to 4 times higher when treatment wasn't finished (about 69 against 17, and 84 against 26 a year per 1,000). The third, which counted only the first 4 weeks, found no clear difference.
